body.text: The Philippines and Australia signed a defense pact yesterday that will boost military cooperation between the two nations, in particular by streamlining the bureaucratic processes involved in joint military activities.

The Defense Cooperation Agreement (DCA), which builds on a number of existing defense accords, was signed in a ceremony on board an Australian naval vessel docked in Manila. The pact will enhance the development of military infrastructure and maritime awareness and information sharing, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said after the ceremony.

“These activities will contribute to making our region more safe, more secure and more prosperous,” he said. “Together with the Philippines and our regional partners we are strengthening maritime resilience and security that helps underpin a peaceful, stable and prosperous region.”

Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro added that the new agreement would cut back the red tape involved in the implementation of the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA), which governs the deployment of Philippine and Australian military personnel while temporarily visiting the other country’s territory. “Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10,” Teodoro told reporters, as per Reuters.

He said the arrangement would pave the way for closer cooperation of the two nations’ maritime, air, and land forces, as well as humanitarian and disaster response. It would also bolster the Philippines’ “credible deterrence posture,” including in its portions of the South China Sea, into which China has in recent years increased both the frequency and intensity of its incursions.

Recent tensions have centered on Scarborough Shoal, a reef due west of Luzon, and Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands, where Manila maintains a small occupying force aboard a grounded warship. This has prompted a series of dangerous confrontations in which the China Coast Guard has rammed Philippine civilian and coast guard vessels and doused them with high-pressure water cannons. In some cases, Philippine and Chinese personal have even exchanged physical blows.
The growing Chinese pressure has had the predictable effect of pushing the Philippines into closer alignment of partners and allies who share its concerns about China’s growing maritime power.

Australia is among the oldest members of this group, having signed the SOVFA with the Philippines in 2007 – the first agreement of its sort of any nation aside from the Visiting Forces Agreement signed between the Philippines and U.S. in 1998. Similar agreements have since been signed with Japan (July 2024), New Zealand (April 2025), Canada (November 2025), and France (March 2026), with negotiations also underway with the United Kingdom.

These agreements have provided the legal scaffolding for a marked increase in joint maritime and coast guard patrols and military exercises known as Maritime Cooperative Activities (MCAs), which now take place regularly in the waters around the Philippines The 20th MCA was held between the Philippines, U.S., and Canada in the Sulu Sea in mid-September.

The growing cooperation has also taken “minilateral” form. The past few years have seen the emergence of a defense bloc of four nations – Australia, the U.S., the Philippines and Japan – nicknamed “the Squad,” which is working together to bolster the Philippines’ defensive capability in an attempt to counter China’s maritime influence in the South and East China seas.

After a meeting of “Squad” defense chiefs in Cebu on October 28, the four nations announced that they would have agreed to establish a coordination hub in the Philippines and to synchronize efforts to strengthen the nation’s defenses.

During their meeting, the Squad defense chiefs expressed their “serious concerns about the situations in the East China Sea and the South China Sea.” They also raised opposition to “any unilateral actions, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability.”
In recent years, Australia has also invested in defense infrastructure at a series of bases across the Philippines, and also providing various forms of support for the Philippine Coast Guard.

The signing of the DCA took place as the Philippines opened the 49th ASEAN Summit and related meetings in Manila, during which the South China Sea disputes were again likely to feature prominently – as they did at the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting in Cebu last month.

In a related announcement yesterday, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro told the press that China and ASEAN had been unable to conclude negotiations on a long-delayed Code of Conduct (COC) for the South China Sea under the Philippines’ chairmanship this year.

The Code is intended to reduce the risk of conflict in the important waterway, where China’s expansive “nine-dash line” maritime claim clashes with those of four ASEAN member states: Vietnam, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Brunei.

The Philippines had pledged to complete the negotiations during its chairmanship but Lazaro said that several key issues remain unresolved, including questions over whether the Code would be legally binding.
“There is no conclusion yet,” she said, adding that “the ASEAN countries plus China have also different views on how things are.”

In a separate statement about the Code, the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said that the two sides had reached agreement on “over 80 percent of the paragraphs of the draft COC.” The DFA said that the parties to the Code “agree to continue to work constructively, with a view to concluding the negotiations on an effective and substantive COC at the earliest possible time.”
